subject: typescript
title: Utility types
description: Partial, Required, Pick, Omit, Record and ReturnType — deriving types instead of repeating them.

content.title: Definition
content.body: Utility types transform an existing type into a related one. Deriving beats duplicating: when the source type changes, everything built from it follows automatically.

content.title: The four you reach for most
content.body: Partial for patch payloads, Pick and Omit for trimmed views, Record for lookups.

content.title: Watch out
content.body: Partial is shallow and Omit accepts keys that do not exist without complaining. Pick is the stricter choice when you want a typo to fail.

exercises.question: What does Partial<User> produce for `interface User { id: string; name: string }`?

answers.text: { id: string | undefined; name: string | undefined }
Partial<{ id: string; name: string }> is not a valid type

exercises.explanation: Partial maps every property to optional. Note that optional and `| undefined` are not the same thing under exactOptionalPropertyTypes.

exercises.question: Which reason favours Pick over Omit?

answers.text: Omit only removes one key at a time
Omit cannot be used with interfaces
Pick lists what stays, so a renamed source property breaks the derived type instead of silently widening it

exercises.explanation: Omit's key parameter is not constrained to keyof T, so a stale key is accepted quietly. Pick's is, and it fails loudly.

exercises.question: Complete the type for a lookup from level name to a list of lessons.
exercises.explanation: Record<K, V> builds an object type with the given key union and value type. Map is a runtime class, not a type utility.

exercises.question: What is the type of R?
exercises.explanation: typeof makeUser is the function type; ReturnType extracts what it resolves to. This is how you avoid writing the shape twice.

exercises.question: Partial<T> makes nested object properties optional as well.
exercises.explanation: Partial is one level deep. A recursive DeepPartial has to be written by hand — or, better, avoided.

exercises.question: Complete the type that is the union of a type's property names.
exercises.explanation: keyof User gives "id" | "name" | "email". typeof works on values, not on types.

exercises.question: Why does this compile even though it is wrong?
exercises.code:
interface User { id: string; name: string }

type Public = Omit<User, "emial">;

answers.text: Omit creates the missing property instead
Omit's key parameter is not constrained to keyof User, so the typo is accepted and nothing is removed
Omit ignores its second argument entirely

exercises.explanation: This is a well-known sharp edge. Pick<User, "id" | "name"> or a constrained helper catches the typo instead.

exercises.question: TypeScript · utility types
exercises.back: Removes null and undefined from a union
exercises.explanation: Equivalent to T & {} in modern TypeScript. Useful after a filter that the compiler cannot follow.

exercises.question: What does Readonly<T> do?

answers.text: Makes the type immutable all the way down
Marks every property readonly, one level deep

exercises.explanation: Like Partial, it is shallow, and it is a compile-time constraint only — Object.freeze is the runtime counterpart.

exercises.question: What is the type of R?
exercises.explanation: Awaited unwraps a promise, recursively. Pairing it with ReturnType is the standard way to name what an async function resolves to.

exercises.question: What does Exclude<'a' | 'b' | 'c', 'b'> produce?
exercises.explanation: Exclude removes assignable members from a union; Extract keeps them. Both are conditional types that distribute over the union.

exercises.question: Complete the mapped type that makes every property nullable.
exercises.code: type Nullable<T> = { [K ___ keyof T]: T[K] | null };
exercises.explanation: `in keyof T` iterates the keys. Partial, Required and Readonly are all written this way, with a +/- modifier on the optional or readonly flag.

exercises.question: Parameters<typeof fn> produces a tuple of the function's parameter types.
exercises.explanation: A tuple, not a union — so Parameters<typeof fn>[0] is the first parameter. Handy for wrapping a function without repeating its signature.

exercises.question: Why does line 2 fail?
exercises.code:
1  type ByLevel = Record<'beginner' | 'advanced', number>;
2  const counts: ByLevel = { beginner: 1 };

answers.text: Record requires a string index signature
Every key of the union is required — advanced is missing
The value type should be a union
Record cannot take a literal union as its key

exercises.explanation: Record over a finite union is exhaustive by design, which is what makes it useful for lookup tables. Partial<ByLevel> if the gaps are intentional.

exercises.question: What does `type Event = `on${Capitalize<'click' | 'focus'>}`` produce?
exercises.explanation: Template literal types distribute over unions and compose with the intrinsic case helpers — the basis of typed event maps and prop name mapping.
